consequence: It enables general private computation in the cloud.

title: BB84 Quantum Key Distribution
subject: Cryptography & Security
statement: The BB84 protocol distributes a secret key using photons prepared in two complementary bases, with eavesdropping detectable through increased error rates.
short: Quantum measurement disturbs the signal in a detectable way.
detail: After basis reconciliation, error estimation, and privacy amplification, the parties obtain a shared key whose security rests on quantum mechanics.
proof: An adversary cannot distinguish nonorthogonal states without disturbance; the no-cloning theorem prevents perfect copying, so intercept-resend introduces errors.
consequence: It provides information-theoretically secure key distribution under quantum assumptions.

title: The One-Time Pad and Perfect Secrecy
subject: Cryptography & Security
statement: XORing a message with a truly random key as long as the message and used only once gives perfect secrecy: the ciphertext reveals no information about the plaintext.
short: A random key of message length makes every plaintext equally likely.
detail: Shannon proved that perfect secrecy requires the key space to be at least as large as the message space.
proof: For any plaintext m and ciphertext c there is exactly one key mapping m to c, so the posterior distribution of m equals the prior.
consequence: It is the only unconditionally secure cipher but requires impractical key management.

title: Kerckhoffs's Principle
subject: Cryptography & Security
statement: A cryptosystem should remain secure even if everything about the algorithm is public, with secrecy residing solely in the key.
latex: security depends on key, not algorithm
short: Security through obscurity is not security.
detail: Open designs can be analysed by the community and still be secure if the key is strong.
proof: If security depended on algorithm secrecy, any leak would break all users at once, whereas keys can be changed individually.
consequence: It is the standard design criterion for modern cryptographic primitives.

title: Semantic Security and IND-CPA
subject: Cryptography & Security
statement: Semantic security requires that a ciphertext reveal no efficiently computable information about its plaintext; under chosen-plaintext attack this is equivalent to indistinguishability of encryptions of two chosen messages.
short: An attacker cannot tell which of two messages was encrypted.
detail: Encryption must be randomized, because deterministic encryption reveals equality of plaintexts.
proof: Indistinguishability of challenge ciphertexts implies no partial information can be extracted efficiently, and vice versa.
consequence: It is the baseline security notion for public-key encryption.

title: Chosen-Ciphertext Security
subject: Cryptography & Security
statement: IND-CCA security requires that an adversary with access to a decryption oracle for all ciphertexts except the challenge still cannot distinguish which of two messages was encrypted.
short: Security must hold even when the attacker can ask for decryptions.
detail: CCA security is stronger than CPA security and is achieved by schemes such as RSA-OAEP under suitable assumptions.
proof: Definition; a CCA attacker could otherwise manipulate ciphertexts and learn relationships about the challenge plaintext.
consequence: It is the practical standard for encryption exposed to active adversaries.

title: The Random Oracle Model
subject: Cryptography & Security
statement: The random oracle model treats a hash function as a truly random function accessible to all parties, and proofs in this model do not automatically transfer to concrete hash functions.
short: A convenient idealization can hide real-world weaknesses.
detail: Canetti, Goldreich, and Halevi constructed schemes provably secure in the random oracle model but insecure for every efficient instantiation.
proof: The separation result constructs a scheme whose behaviour is subverted whenever the oracle is replaced by a concrete algorithm.
consequence: Random-oracle proofs are useful evidence but not unconditional guarantees.

title: Digital Signatures and One-Way Functions
subject: Cryptography & Security
statement: Digest digital signatures exist if and only if one-way functions exist.
short: Signatures are possible exactly when one-way functions are.
detail: The forward direction builds signatures from one-way functions via one-time signatures and trees; the reverse is immediate since a signature scheme yields a one-way function.
proof: Construct one-time signature schemes and chain them using a hash tree to sign many messages; conversely, signing is easy but forging is hard.
consequence: It places signatures at the foundation of cryptography.

title: Message Authentication Codes
subject: Cryptography & Security
statement: A message authentication code is a keyed function producing a tag that lets a holder of the shared key verify both integrity and origin of a message.
short: A shared secret key certifies that a message was not altered.
detail: Unlike digital signatures, MACs are symmetric and do not provide non-repudiation.
proof: Definition; unforgeability means no efficient adversary can produce a valid tag for a new message without the key.
consequence: MACs protect message integrity in almost every network protocol.

title: Merkle Trees
subject: Cryptography & Security
statement: A Merkle tree hashes pairs of leaf hashes recursively so that a single root hash authenticates an entire collection of data.
short: One hash can vouch for arbitrarily many records.
detail: Membership proofs require only a logarithmic number of sibling hashes along a path to the root.
proof: Collision resistance of the hash makes changing any leaf change the root unless a collision is found.
consequence: Merkle trees are central to certificates, distributed ledgers, and file systems.

title: Side-Channel Attacks
subject: Cryptography & Security
statement: A side-channel attack recovers secrets from physical implementation details such as timing, power consumption, electromagnetic emissions, or cache behaviour rather than from flaws in the abstract algorithm.
latex: secret leaked via time, power, EM, cache
short: Correct mathematics can still leak through the hardware that runs it.
detail: Countermeasures include constant-time code, masking, and blinding.
proof: Measurements correlated with secret-dependent operations reveal information statistically; empirical and information-theoretic analyses quantify the leakage.
consequence: Secure implementations require attention beyond algorithmic proofs.

title: The Lambda Calculus
subject: Programming Languages
statement: The lambda calculus is a formal system whose terms are variables, abstractions, and applications, with computation expressed by beta reduction.
short: Functions are the only data, and applying one is the only computation step.
detail: Both untyped and typed variants exist; the untyped version can encode ordinary data as functions.
proof: Define the syntax and the capture-avoiding substitution rule that implements beta reduction.
consequence: It is the theoretical core of functional programming languages.

title: Church–Rosser Confluence of Beta Reduction
subject: Programming Languages
statement: Beta reduction in the lambda calculus is confluent: if a term reduces to two different terms, there is a common term to which both can further reduce.
latex: M →* N₁ and M →* N₂ imply ∃ P : N₁ →* P, N₂ →* P
short: The order of reductions cannot change the final answer if one exists.
detail: Confluence together with normalization yields uniqueness of normal forms up to alpha equivalence.
proof: Verify local confluence by analysing critical pairs and apply the diamond property of parallel reduction.
consequence: It justifies evaluating lambda terms without specifying a reduction strategy.

title: Strong Normalization of Simply Typed Lambda Calculus
subject: Programming Languages
statement: Every well-typed term of the simply typed lambda calculus terminates: there is no infinite sequence of beta reduction steps.
latex: ⊢ M : τ implies M is strongly normalizing
short: Types rule out nonterminating computation in this language.
detail: The result fails for the untyped calculus, where the omega combinator loops forever.
proof: Assign to each type a set of reducibility candidates and show by induction on types that every well-typed term belongs to its candidate set.
consequence: It shows that a type discipline can guarantee termination.

title: The Simply Typed Lambda Calculus
subject: Programming Languages
statement: The simply typed lambda calculus enriches lambda abstraction with a type annotation for the argument and a type system that rejects self-application.
short: Functions carry the type of what they accept and what they return.
detail: It has function types and base types but no polymorphism, and all its well-typed programs terminate.
proof: Define typing rules for variables, abstraction, and application; the standard derivation system enforces type correctness.
consequence: It is the minimal typed language underlying most type systems.

title: The Curry–Howard Correspondence
subject: Programming Languages
statement: Propositions correspond to types and proofs correspond to programs, so proof normalization corresponds to program execution.
short: A proof is a program and its proposition is the program's type.
detail: Implication corresponds to function types, conjunction to products, and disjunction to sums.
proof: Check that natural deduction rules match the introduction and elimination rules of the corresponding type constructors.
consequence: It unifies logic and programming language design.

title: System F and Impredicative Polymorphism
subject: Programming Languages
statement: System F extends the simply typed lambda calculus with universal quantification over types and type abstraction, allowing a term to be used at all types.
short: A single definition can be genuinely polymorphic over every type.
detail: The identity function can be given the principal type for all alpha; System F is impredicative because a quantified type may itself be instantiated with a quantified type.
proof: Add type abstraction and type application rules; Girard's reducibility proof establishes strong normalization.
consequence: It underlies parametric polymorphism in languages such as ML and Haskell.

title: Untyped Lambda Calculus Is Turing Complete
subject: Programming Languages
statement: The untyped lambda calculus can encode natural numbers, booleans, lists, recursion, and every partial recursive function.
short: Functions alone suffice to express any computation.
detail: Church numerals encode numbers as iterated functions, and fixed-point combinators supply recursion.
proof: Encode the standard primitives and show how to simulate the μ-recursive functions, which equal the Turing-computable ones.
consequence: It establishes equivalence between two foundational models of computation.

title: Fixed-Point Combinators
subject: Programming Languages
statement: In the untyped lambda calculus a fixed-point combinator Y satisfies Y F reducing to F (Y F), enabling recursive definitions without named self-reference.
latex: Y = λf. (λx. f (x x)) (λx. f (x x))
short: Self-application turns any function into a recursive one.
detail: Typed calculi need an explicit recursive type or a primitive fixpoint because Y is not typable in simple types.
proof: Substitute the definition of Y and reduce one beta step to obtain F (Y F).
consequence: It explains how recursion is implemented in languages that lack recursive definitions.

title: Call-by-Value versus Call-by-Name
subject: Programming Languages
statement: Call-by-value evaluates an argument before applying a function, while call-by-name passes the unevaluated expression and substitutes it when needed.
latex: CBV: evaluate argument; CBN: delay argument
short: Evaluation order decides when, or whether, an argument is computed.
detail: A function ignoring its argument terminates under call-by-name on a diverging argument but diverges under call-by-value; side effects make the choice observable.
proof: Consider the term (λx. 1) Ω where Ω is a diverging term: call-by-name reduces to 1, call-by-value must evaluate Ω first.
consequence: Evaluation strategy is a semantic design decision, not merely an implementation detail.

title: Small-Step and Big-Step Operational Semantics
subject: Programming Languages
statement: Small-step semantics describes individual computation steps via a transition relation, while big-step semantics relates an expression directly to its final value.
short: One style zooms into each step; the other summarizes the whole run.
detail: Small-step semantics handles concurrency and divergence more naturally; big-step semantics is often simpler for expression languages.
proof: Define rules inductively for each construct; big-step derivations can be recovered from sequences of small steps for deterministic languages.
consequence: The choice of semantic style affects which properties are easy to prove.

title: Denotational Semantics
subject: Programming Languages
statement: Denotational semantics assigns mathematical objects, typically elements of Scott domains, to programs compositionally so that the meaning of a compound is a function of the meanings of its parts.
short: Programs denote mathematical values built from the meanings of their pieces.
detail: Domains with partial order and limits of chains model nontermination via a bottom element.
proof: Define semantic functions by structural recursion on syntax and use fixed-point operators for recursion.
consequence: It supports equational reasoning and the design of language features.

title: Hoare Triples and Axiomatic Semantics
subject: Programming Languages
statement: A Hoare triple {P} C {Q} asserts that if precondition P holds before command C and C terminates, then postcondition Q holds afterwards.
short: Reason about programs using logical assertions before and after each command.
detail: Rules for assignment, sequencing, conditionals, and loops allow compositional correctness proofs; total correctness additionally requires termination.
proof: The assignment axiom substitutes the assigned expression into the postcondition; the loop rule uses an invariant preserved by each iteration.
consequence: It is the basis of deductive program verification.

title: Closures and Lexical Environments
subject: Programming Languages
statement: A closure is a function bundled with the lexical environment in which it was created, so it can refer to variables from that scope after the scope has exited.
short: A function remembers the variables that were in scope when it was defined.
detail: Closures are the standard implementation of first-class functions with lexical scoping and are essential for callbacks and iterators.
proof: At closure creation, capture bindings for all free variables; applying the closure extends the saved environment with its parameters.
consequence: They enable higher-order programming and compact event-driven code.

title: Lexical versus Dynamic Scoping
subject: Programming Languages
statement: Under lexical scoping a free variable is resolved in the environment where the function was defined; under dynamic scoping it is resolved in the caller's environment.
latex: lexical: definition site; dynamic: call site
short: The same name can mean different things depending on where a function was written.
detail: Most modern languages use lexical scoping because it makes reasoning about programs local; dynamic scoping was common in early Lisp dialects.
proof: Implement lexical scope by closures and dynamic scope by a global stack of active bindings.
consequence: The choice affects modularity and the behaviour of higher-order functions.

title: Garbage Collection
subject: Programming Languages
statement: Garbage collection automatically reclaims memory occupied by objects that can no longer be reached from program roots.
short: The runtime frees memory the program can no longer use.
detail: The two main families are tracing collectors, which follow references from roots, and reference counting, which tracks incoming references.
proof: Compute the transitive closure of references from roots and reclaim every object outside it; unreachable objects can never be accessed again.
consequence: It removes manual memory management errors but introduces runtime overhead and pauses.

title: Mark-and-Sweep Collection
subject: Programming Languages
statement: Mark-and-sweep collection traverses all objects reachable from roots marking them, then sweeps the heap reclaiming unmarked objects.
short: Two passes separate live objects from garbage.
detail: Variants include tri-colouring and incremental collection to reduce pause times.
proof: Starting from roots, follow every outgoing reference and set a mark bit; any object without a mark cannot be reached, so its memory can be reused.
consequence: It is a simple and robust collector that handles cyclic garbage.

title: Generational Garbage Collection
subject: Programming Languages
statement: Generational collectors divide objects by age and collect young objects more often, exploiting the empirical fact that most objects die soon after allocation.
short: Recent objects are the most likely garbage.
detail: Minor collections scan a small young region; survivors are promoted to an older region collected rarely.
proof: Write barriers record references from old to young objects so a minor collection can find all roots of the young generation without scanning the whole heap.
consequence: It greatly reduces collection cost in typical workloads.

title: Reference Counting Fails on Cyclic Garbage
subject: Programming Languages
statement: Pure reference counting cannot reclaim a cycle of objects that reference only one another, because each object still has a positive reference count.
short: Mutually referential objects keep each other alive forever.
detail: Tracing collectors handle cycles naturally, and hybrid schemes use cycle detection for reference-counted heaps.
proof: In a two-node cycle each node's only reference comes from the other, so no count reaches zero and no object is freed.
consequence: It explains why production collectors usually combine tracing with counting.

title: Compilation versus Interpretation
subject: Programming Languages
statement: A compiler translates a whole program to another language before execution, while an interpreter executes the source program step by step.
latex: source → compiler → target; interpreter executes source
short: Translate ahead of time or translate while running.
detail: Modern implementations often mix the two, using bytecode compiled ahead of time and a just-in-time compiler at runtime.
proof: Both approaches implement the same semantics; they differ in when translation occurs and how much runtime information is available.
consequence: The tradeoff affects portability, startup time, and peak performance.

title: Compiler Phase Structure
subject: Programming Languages
statement: A compiler is typically organized as lexical analysis, syntax analysis, semantic analysis, intermediate-code generation, optimization, and target-code generation.
latex: source → tokens → AST → IR → machine code
short: Translation proceeds through successively more structured representations.
detail: The front end depends mainly on the source language and the back end mainly on the target architecture.
proof: Define each phase's input and output; composition of correct phases yields a correct compiler.
consequence: Modular phases allow retargeting and reuse of front ends.

title: Abstract Syntax Trees
subject: Programming Languages
statement: An abstract syntax tree represents the hierarchical syntactic structure of a program while omitting incidental punctuation and concrete syntax details.
short: A tree that keeps meaning but drops formatting noise.
detail: ASTs are the interface between parsing and semantic analysis and are the basis of most source-level tools.
proof: Build a node for each grammar production used in a parse and discard tokens such as parentheses that serve only disambiguation.
consequence: They enable type checking, transformations, and code generation.

title: Regular Expressions in Lexical Analysis
subject: Programming Languages
statement: Lexical tokens such as identifiers and numbers are specified by regular expressions and recognized by finite automata generated from them.
short: The lexer is a finite-state machine built from token patterns.
detail: Longest-match rules and token priority resolve ambiguities between patterns.
proof: Convert each regular expression to an NFA by Thompson's construction, combine them, and determinize for fast scanning.
consequence: It connects formal language theory to practical compiler construction.

title: LR Parsing
subject: Programming Languages
statement: LR parsing is a bottom-up shift-reduce parsing technique that builds a rightmost derivation in reverse using a deterministic stack automaton.
short: Reduce a string to the start symbol by recognizing handles on a stack.
detail: LALR and SLR are practical variants with smaller parse tables; LR(1) handles the broadest class of deterministic context-free grammars.
proof: Construct item sets representing parser states and derive shift and reduce actions from the LR automaton.
consequence: Most programming language grammars are parsed by LR-style generators.

title: LL Parsing
subject: Programming Languages
statement: LL parsing is a top-down technique that expands the leftmost nonterminal using a fixed lookahead to choose a production.
latex: predict production from first k tokens
short: Start from the grammar's start symbol and expand leftmost symbols.
detail: Recursive descent parsers implement LL grammars directly; left recursion must be eliminated.
proof: Compute FIRST and FOLLOW sets to determine which production applies for each lookahead token.
consequence: It is easy to implement by hand for many languages.

title: Static Single Assignment Form
subject: Programming Languages
statement: In static single assignment form each variable is assigned exactly once, and control-flow merges use phi functions to select among reaching definitions.
short: Every value gets a unique name, making data flow explicit.
detail: SSA simplifies optimizations such as constant propagation and dead-code elimination.
proof: Rename variables so each definition has a fresh name and insert phi nodes at dominance frontiers of multiple definitions.
consequence: It is the intermediate representation of choice in optimizing compilers.

title: Dataflow Analysis as a Fixed-Point Problem
subject: Programming Languages
statement: Classical dataflow analyses compute a fixed point of monotone transfer functions over a finite lattice of facts along a control-flow graph.
latex: entry and join transfer iteration to fixed point
short: Repeatedly propagate facts until nothing changes.
detail: Examples include reaching definitions, live variables, and available expressions; monotonicity guarantees convergence.
proof: Model each program point's fact as a lattice element and apply transfer functions iteratively; Tarski's fixed-point theorem gives the least or greatest fixed point.
consequence: It gives a uniform framework for sound static analyses.

title: The Monad Laws
subject: Programming Languages
statement: A monad consists of a type constructor with return and bind operations satisfying left identity, right identity, and associativity.
latex: return a >>= f = f a; m >>= return = m
short: Monads compose effectful computations in a predictable way.
detail: The laws ensure that rewriting nested binds does not change program meaning, which enables equational reasoning and compiler optimizations.
proof: Check the three laws from the definitions for a given monad, such as the maybe or list monad.
consequence: They give a uniform interface for effects in pure functional languages.

title: Monads and Effectful Computation
subject: Programming Languages
statement: Monads model effects such as state, exceptions, nondeterminism, and input-output inside a purely functional language by sequencing computations that produce wrapped values.
latex: IO a, State s a, Maybe a
short: Effects are expressed as values with a disciplined way to chain them.
detail: Each monad captures a different effect while preserving referential transparency of the underlying language.
proof: Define return to inject a pure value and bind to sequence computations, with monad laws ensuring composition behaves like function composition.
consequence: They allow purely functional programs to interact with the world.

title: Algebraic Data Types
subject: Programming Languages
statement: An algebraic data type is built from sum types representing alternatives and product types representing grouped fields.
latex: data T = A | B of α × β
short: Combine alternatives and records to describe structured data.
detail: Examples include lists, trees, and option types; recursive definitions allow infinitely many finite values.
proof: Give formation, introduction, and elimination rules for sums and products; induction follows from the constructors.
consequence: They support exhaustive pattern matching and algebraic reasoning about data.

title: Pattern Matching
subject: Programming Languages
statement: Pattern matching selects a branch of code by comparing a value against structured patterns that may bind variables to subcomponents.
latex: match x with | Some y → … | None → …
short: Destructure data and branch in one step.
detail: Exhaustiveness and redundancy checks can be performed statically for algebraic data types.
proof: Define a matching relation for each pattern form and choose the first branch whose pattern matches the value.
consequence: It makes code over recursive data concise and enables compiler checks of coverage.

title: Type Soundness via Progress and Preservation
subject: Programming Languages
statement: A well-typed program is type sound if it satisfies progress, meaning it is either a value or can take a step, and preservation, meaning each step preserves its type.
latex: progress + preservation ⇒ no type errors at runtime
short: Well-typed programs cannot get stuck.
detail: Wright and Felleisen formulated this approach, which is now the standard way to prove language safety.
proof: Prove progress and preservation by induction on typing derivations, then combine them into a theorem about every evaluation sequence.
consequence: It gives a rigorous meaning to the slogan that well-typed programs cannot go wrong.

title: Subtyping and the Substitution Principle
subject: Programming Languages
statement: Subtyping allows a value of one type to be used wherever a value of a supertype is expected; the Liskov substitution principle requires that this replacement preserve program behaviour.
latex: S <: T means S values can stand for T values
short: A more specific type can safely stand in for a more general one.
detail: Behavioural substitutability constrains precondition and postcondition rules beyond structural subtyping.
proof: A subsumption rule permits using a term of subtype S where T is required; soundness is shown by type preservation.
consequence: It underpins object-oriented languages and interface-based design.

title: Variance of Type Constructors
subject: Programming Languages
statement: A type constructor is covariant if subtyping is preserved, contravariant if it is reversed, and invariant if neither holds.
latex: F covariant: A <: B ⇒ F A <: F B
short: Function arguments reverse subtyping; containers usually preserve it.
detail: Function types are contravariant in their argument and covariant in their result, which explains why mutable arrays must be invariant.
proof: Check soundness of subtyping rules by considering how values of the constructed type are used.
consequence: Variance determines which generic types are safely substitutable.

title: Tail-Call Optimization
subject: Programming Languages
statement: A call in tail position can be implemented as a jump reusing the current stack frame, so a tail-recursive loop uses constant stack space.
latex: tail call → goto with updated arguments
short: The last action of a function need not add a stack frame.
detail: Proper tail recursion is a guarantee in some languages and an optimization in others.
proof: Since no work remains after the call, the caller's frame can be discarded and the callee's parameters placed in its place.
consequence: It lets recursion replace explicit loops without stack overflow.

title: Continuation-Passing Style
subject: Programming Languages
statement: In continuation-passing style every function takes an explicit continuation argument representing the rest of the computation and invokes it with its result.
latex: f(x, k) with k applied to result
short: Make the rest of the program an explicit function argument.
detail: CPS makes evaluation order and control flow explicit, which simplifies compilers and implements exceptions and coroutines.
proof: Transform each expression by giving it a continuation that receives its value; the final result is obtained by applying the identity continuation.
consequence: It is a standard intermediate representation in compilers.

title: Abstract Interpretation
subject: Programming Languages
statement: Abstract interpretation is a framework for sound static analysis in which concrete program semantics are approximated by computations over an abstract domain related by a Galois connection.
latex: concrete semantics α ⇄ γ abstract semantics
short: Analyze an over-approximation of all possible program behaviours.
detail: Interval analysis and sign analysis are classic examples; abstraction trades precision for termination and speed.
proof: Require abstract transfer functions to over-approximate concrete ones and iterate to an abstract fixed point; soundness follows by induction.
consequence: It is the theoretical basis of many industrial static analyzers.

title: The CAP Theorem
subject: Distributed Systems
statement: In a distributed data store that may experience network partitions, a system cannot simultaneously guarantee linearizable consistency and availability; it must sacrifice one when a partition occurs.
short: When messages are lost you must choose between correct answers and any answers.
detail: Gilbert and Lynch proved the theorem for a formal model; availability here means every request to a non-failing node eventually returns.
proof: Partition the network into two groups and issue conflicting updates; a linearizable system must reject one group, violating availability, while an available system must give stale answers.
consequence: It explains the design space of NoSQL databases and tradeoffs during outages.

title: The PACELC Extension
subject: Distributed Systems
statement: PACELC extends CAP by adding that even when the system is running normally, a designer must trade latency against consistency.
latex: if P then A/C else L/C
short: Even without partitions, consistent answers can cost time.
detail: CP systems become unavailable during partitions; AP systems accept stale data; in normal operation systems choose between low latency and strong consistency.
proof: Replicating synchronously to guarantee consistency adds communication delay, so latency and consistency cannot both be minimized.
consequence: It gives a more complete vocabulary for database design.

title: FLP Consensus Impossibility
subject: Distributed Systems
statement: In a fully asynchronous system where one process may crash, no deterministic algorithm can solve consensus.
latex: deterministic consensus impossible with f ≥ 1 crash in async model
short: Without timing assumptions, a single crash can prevent agreement forever.
detail: The result holds even with reliable messages and no Byzantine faults; practical protocols therefore use timeouts, randomization, or partial synchrony.
proof: Fischer, Lynch, and Paterson construct an infinite execution that can be extended either to a decision on zero or on one by changing when a single process crashes.
consequence: It explains why real consensus protocols rely on eventual timing guarantees.

title: The Paxos Protocol
subject: Distributed Systems
statement: Paxos reaches consensus in an asynchronous network with crash failures using prepare and accept phases and majority quorums, guaranteeing safety regardless of timing.
short: Overlapping majorities prevent two conflicting values from being chosen.
detail: Multi-Paxos elects a stable leader to skip repeated prepare phases; liveness requires eventual synchrony.
proof: A proposer with a higher ballot learns all previously accepted values from a majority, so it cannot overwrite a chosen value; quorum intersection gives uniqueness.
consequence: It is the foundational protocol for replicated state machines.

title: The Raft Consensus Algorithm
subject: Distributed Systems
statement: Raft achieves consensus by electing a strong leader that replicates an ordered log to a majority of followers.
short: Pick one leader and let it order all updates.
detail: Raft is designed for understandability, decomposing consensus into leader election, log replication, and safety.
proof: A candidate wins only with a majority vote, and an entry commits only after replication on a majority, so two leaders cannot commit conflicting entries in the same term.
consequence: It is widely used in production systems such as etcd and Consul.

title: Byzantine Faults
subject: Distributed Systems
statement: A Byzantine fault is an arbitrary failure in which a component may send conflicting or fabricated messages to different peers.
short: The faulty node may actively lie, not merely stop.
detail: Tolerating f Byzantine faults generally requires at least 3f+1 replicas in asynchronous or partially synchronous settings.
proof: Lower bounds follow from distinguishing two worlds whose message patterns can be simulated by f traitors; three-f-plus-one is achievable by PBFT-style protocols.
consequence: It is essential for safety-critical and blockchain systems.

title: The Byzantine Generals Problem
subject: Distributed Systems
statement: The Byzantine generals problem asks loyal commanders to agree on a common action despite traitors among them who may send contradictory messages.
latex: agreement with f traitors needs 3f+1 generals
short: Reaching agreement when some participants may lie.
detail: Oral messages require more than two thirds loyal for agreement; signed messages improve the bound.
proof: Lamport, Shostak, and Pease showed impossibility for three generals with one traitor and gave algorithms for sufficiently many loyal generals.
consequence: It is the canonical abstraction of Byzantine agreement.

title: Practical Byzantine Fault Tolerance
subject: Distributed Systems
statement: PBFT replicas all run the same state machine and tolerate f Byzantine faults using three-f-plus-one replicas and pre-prepare, prepare, and commit phases.
short: Three phases of message exchange let honest replicas agree despite liars.
detail: A primary orders requests and backups verify and exchange signed messages; view changes replace a faulty primary.
proof: Prepared and committed certificates require two-f-plus-one matching messages, and the intersection of such sets contains an honest replica that prevents conflicting commits.
consequence: It made Byzantine agreement practical for modest-size systems.

title: The Two-Phase Commit Protocol
subject: Distributed Systems
statement: Two-phase commit coordinates an atomic transaction across several databases using a prepare phase followed by a commit or abort phase.
short: Ask everyone if they can commit, then tell everyone the decision.
detail: If the coordinator crashes after participants have voted yes but before deciding, participants may remain blocked indefinitely.
proof: Every participant records a prepared decision and promises to follow the coordinator's final instruction; atomicity follows from the coordinator's single global decision.
consequence: It is the classic atomic commitment protocol despite its blocking failure mode.

title: Three-Phase Commit
subject: Distributed Systems
statement: Three-phase commit adds a pre-commit phase to two-phase commit so that participants can decide without the coordinator if it fails after all participants have pre-committed.
short: An extra stage removes the indefinite blocking of two-phase commit.
detail: The protocol is non-blocking only under bounded message delays and no network partitions; it is unsafe under arbitrary partitions.
proof: Once every participant is pre-committed, the final commit is safe because all participants know the global decision was made.
consequence: It illustrates the tradeoff between liveness and assumptions about the network.

title: Eventual Consistency
subject: Distributed Systems
statement: Eventual consistency guarantees that if no new updates are made, all replicas will eventually converge to the same value.
short: Replicas may disagree temporarily but catch up in the absence of new writes.
detail: It allows low-latency writes during partitions and is formalised by convergence and strong eventual consistency variants using CRDTs.
proof: Assume all updates are eventually propagated; after the last update, anti-entropy spreads it to every replica, so states agree.
consequence: It is the consistency model of many large-scale web systems.

title: Linearizability
subject: Distributed Systems
statement: Linearizability requires that every operation appears to take effect atomically at some instant between its invocation and response, consistent with real-time order.
short: A concurrent object behaves as if each operation happened at one instant.
detail: It is a strong single-object consistency condition and is compositional: combining linearizable objects yields a linearizable system.
proof: Choose a linearization point within each operation interval so the resulting sequential history respects the object's specification.
consequence: It is the formal meaning of strong consistency in databases.

title: Sequential Consistency
subject: Distributed Systems
statement: Sequential consistency requires that the result of any execution be the same as if operations were executed in some sequential order respecting each process's program order.
short: All processes see a single order of operations, but it need not respect real time.
detail: It is weaker than linearizability because it does not constrain operations whose intervals do not overlap.
proof: Construct a total order extending each process's program order and check that the observed values match a sequential execution.
consequence: It is a standard model for shared-memory multiprocessors.

title: Causal Consistency
subject: Distributed Systems
statement: Causal consistency requires that operations related by potential causality be seen in the same order by all processes, while concurrent operations may be observed in different orders.
latex: a → b implies all processes see a before b
short: Keep cause before effect; allow reordering of unrelated events.
detail: Vector clocks are commonly used to track the causal dependencies that must be preserved.
proof: Tag operations with causal contexts and deliver an operation only after all operations it depends on have been delivered.
consequence: It offers a practical middle ground between eventual and strong consistency.

title: The Happened-Before Relation
subject: Distributed Systems
statement: An event a happened before an event b if they are in the same process with a earlier, or if a is a send of a message received before b, or by transitive closure of these rules.
short: Causality is defined by program order and message order.
detail: Events unrelated by happened-before are concurrent, so their relative order can be chosen arbitrarily without changing observable behaviour.
proof: Define the relation on process-local events and message send-receive pairs, then take its transitive closure.
consequence: It is the foundation of logical time and causal consistency.

title: Lamport Logical Clocks
subject: Distributed Systems
statement: Lamport clocks assign timestamps so that if event a happened before event b then the timestamp of a is less than that of b, by incrementing a local counter and carrying the sender's timestamp with messages.
short: Counters order causes but cannot identify concurrency.
detail: The converse fails: equal or ordered timestamps do not imply a happens-before relationship.
proof: Increment the counter at each event and on receive set it to one plus the maximum of local and received timestamps.
consequence: They provide a simple total order extension for distributed events.

title: Vector Clocks
subject: Distributed Systems
statement: Vector clocks maintain one counter per process so that one timestamp is less than another exactly when the corresponding event happened before it.
short: A vector of counters captures causality exactly.
detail: Incomparable vectors identify concurrent events, which is essential for conflict detection in replicated stores.
proof: Each process increments its own component and merges by componentwise maximum on receive; induction on the happens-before relation gives the equivalence.
consequence: They are used for versioning and conflict detection in distributed databases.

title: Lamport's Bakery Algorithm
subject: Distributed Systems
statement: The bakery algorithm provides mutual exclusion for n processes using only atomic reads and writes, assigning each process a ticket and serving tickets in numeric order.
short: Take a numbered ticket and wait your turn.
detail: It assumes atomic single-word reads and writes and remains correct even if processes crash outside the critical section only with extra care.
proof: Ticket numbers are unique and increasing; a process with the smallest ticket cannot be blocked by a process holding a larger one.
consequence: It shows mutual exclusion is possible without special atomic instructions.

title: Leader Election and the Bully Algorithm
subject: Distributed Systems
statement: The bully algorithm elects a coordinator by letting a process that detects a missing leader challenge higher-identified processes, with the highest live identifier winning.
short: A process challenges everyone it outranks and withdraws if a stronger one answers.
detail: It assumes synchronous message delivery and known process identifiers; ring algorithms are an alternative.
proof: Any process can initiate an election; only a process that hears no response from higher identifiers declares itself leader and broadcasts the result.
consequence: Leader election is a primitive for many coordinated distributed services.

title: Token-Ring Mutual Exclusion
subject: Distributed Systems
statement: In a token-ring algorithm a single token circulates among processes, and only the holder of the token may enter the critical section.
short: Ownership of a rotating token grants permission to enter.
detail: Token loss or duplication must be handled by a recovery mechanism.
proof: Since exactly one token exists, at most one process can hold it and enter the critical section at any time.
consequence: It gives a simple distributed mutual exclusion scheme with bounded waiting.

title: Quorum Systems for Replicated Data
subject: Distributed Systems
statement: A quorum system is a family of intersecting subsets of replicas; requiring write quorums to intersect read quorums prevents a read from missing the latest write.
latex: R + W > N and W > N/2
short: Any read set must overlap any write set.
detail: Strict majority quorums are the simplest example; weighted and grid quorums trade availability against size.
proof: If R plus W exceeds N, a read quorum and a write quorum must share a replica, which holds the most recent version.
consequence: Quorums are the backbone of replicated storage protocols.

title: Gossip Protocols
subject: Distributed Systems
statement: Gossip protocols spread information by having each node periodically exchange state with randomly chosen peers, analogous to epidemic spread.
short: Tell a few neighbours, and let them tell others.
detail: They are robust to failures and scale well, with dissemination time typically logarithmic in the number of nodes.
proof: Model dissemination as an epidemic process; each round multiplies the number of informed nodes until nearly all are informed with high probability.
consequence: They are used for membership, failure detection, and anti-entropy in large clusters.

title: Atomic Broadcast
subject: Distributed Systems
statement: Atomic broadcast delivers every message to all correct processes in the same total order, or to none of them.
short: Everyone receives the same messages in the same order.
detail: Atomic broadcast is equivalent to consensus in asynchronous systems with crash failures.
proof: Implement it by agreeing on a sequence of messages using consensus; conversely, consensus can be reduced to atomic broadcast.
consequence: It is the abstraction behind replicated state machines.

title: Failure Detectors and Consensus
subject: Distributed Systems
statement: Chandra and Toueg showed that the eventually perfect failure detector diamond-P is sufficient to solve consensus in an otherwise asynchronous crash-prone system.
short: A sufficiently accurate suspicion mechanism sidesteps FLP.
detail: Failure detectors are characterized by completeness and accuracy properties; diamond-P eventually stops suspecting correct processes and eventually suspects every crashed one.
proof: Use the detector to elect a leader with a rotating coordinator; after the detector stabilises, a majority of correct processes forms and decides.
consequence: It gives a clean abstraction separating timing assumptions from consensus logic.

title: State Machine Replication
subject: Distributed Systems
statement: State machine replication makes a service fault tolerant by running identical deterministic replicas that process the same sequence of requests in the same order.
short: Many copies of one deterministic machine behave as one.
detail: The main challenge is agreeing on the request order, which is what consensus protocols provide.
proof: If replicas start in the same state and apply the same sequence of deterministic transitions, induction gives identical states after each step.
consequence: It is the standard architecture for fault-tolerant services.

title: The Two Generals' Problem
subject: Distributed Systems
statement: Two armies communicating over an unreliable link cannot reach certain agreement on an attack time, because the last acknowledgement in any finite exchange may be lost.
short: No finite number of confirmations can make both sides certain.
detail: It is an early illustration of the impossibility that FLP later generalized to crash-prone asynchronous systems.
proof: For any protocol, consider the last message; if it is lost, the sender cannot know the receiver received it, so certainty fails.
consequence: It motivates acknowledgements with timeouts and probabilistic guarantees in real protocols.

title: Synchrony Models in Distributed Computing
subject: Distributed Systems
statement: Distributed systems are analysed under synchronous models with known bounds, asynchronous models with no bounds, and partially synchronous models where bounds hold eventually or are unknown.
short: What you assume about time determines what you can solve.
detail: Consensus is solvable with crashes in synchronous and partially synchronous models but not in the fully asynchronous one.
proof: Define bounds on message delay and relative process speed for each model and observe their effect on FLP-style arguments.
consequence: The choice of model determines which impossibility results apply.

title: Clock Synchronization Protocols
subject: Distributed Systems
statement: Clock synchronization algorithms such as Cristian's algorithm and NTP estimate remote time by exchanging timestamped messages and compensating for round-trip delay.
short: Measure round-trip delay to estimate another machine's clock.
detail: Physical clocks drift, so synchronization must be repeated; logical clocks address ordering rather than absolute time.
proof: Assume symmetric delays, record send and receive timestamps at both ends, and compute the offset from their differences.
consequence: It supports timestamps, logs, and deadline enforcement across machines.

title: Hamming Distance
subject: Information Theory
statement: The Hamming distance between two equal-length strings is the number of positions at which their symbols differ.
short: Count the coordinates where two words disagree.
detail: It is a genuine metric on strings of fixed length, satisfying nonnegativity, symmetry, and the triangle inequality.
proof: Nonnegativity and symmetry are immediate; the triangle inequality holds coordinatewise because an indicator of x differing from z is at most the sum of the indicators for x versus y and y versus z.
consequence: It is the standard error measure in coding theory.

title: The Hamming Bound
subject: Information Theory
statement: A q-ary code of length n and minimum distance at least 2t+1 has at most q to the n divided by the volume of a Hamming ball of radius t codewords.
short: Error-correcting spheres around codewords cannot overlap.
detail: Codes meeting the bound are called perfect; binary Hamming codes and the binary Golay code are examples.
proof: A code correcting t errors has disjoint radius-t balls around codewords; each ball has the stated volume and all lie in the q-ary Hamming space.
consequence: It gives an upper limit on code size for a desired correction capability.

title: The Singleton Bound
subject: Information Theory
statement: A code of length n and minimum distance d over an alphabet of size q has at most q to the power n minus d plus one codewords.
short: Deleting d minus one positions must leave all codewords distinct.
detail: Codes attaining equality are called maximum distance separable, with Reed–Solomon codes as the main example.
proof: Delete d−1 coordinates from every codeword; two codewords that become equal would differ in at most d−1 positions, contradicting minimum distance d.
consequence: It is a simple and widely used upper bound in coding theory.

title: The Gilbert–Varshamov Bound
subject: Information Theory
statement: There exist q-ary codes of length n and relative distance delta whose rate is at least one minus the q-ary entropy of delta.
short: Greedy construction guarantees codes with reasonably good distance and rate.
detail: It shows that good codes exist even when explicit constructions are unknown, and is tight in a broad asymptotic sense for large alphabets.
proof: Greedily add a word whenever it lies outside the union of balls of radius d−1 around chosen words; volume counting shows the process continues long enough.
consequence: It is a fundamental existence result for error-correcting codes.

title: Linear Codes and Generator Matrices
subject: Information Theory
statement: A linear code is a subspace of the vector space of length-n words over a finite field, and its codewords are obtained by multiplying message vectors by a generator matrix.
short: Codewords form a vector space, so encoding is linear.
detail: The dimension k gives q to the k codewords and the rate k divided by n.
proof: A subspace closed under addition and scalar multiplication is spanned by k independent rows; every codeword is a linear combination of them.
consequence: Linearity makes encoding, decoding, and analysis efficient.

title: Parity-Check Matrices and Syndromes
subject: Information Theory
statement: A parity-check matrix H of a linear code satisfies G H transpose equals zero, and the syndrome of a received word r is H r transpose, which is zero exactly when r is a codeword.
short: A syndrome compresses the error pattern into a small vector.
detail: Decoding can be organized by matching the syndrome to the most likely error pattern.
proof: The rows of H span the orthogonal complement of the code; r is a codeword exactly when r lies in the kernel of H.
consequence: Syndrome decoding is the basis of practical decoders for many codes.

title: Hamming Codes
subject: Information Theory
statement: Binary Hamming codes have parameters n = 2 to the m minus one, k = n minus m, and minimum distance three, allowing correction of any single-bit error.
short: Parity bits indexed by nonzero binary vectors identify the erroneous position.
detail: The syndrome directly gives the index of the flipped bit; extended Hamming codes add an overall parity bit and correct one error while detecting two.
proof: Choose columns of the parity-check matrix to be all distinct nonzero m-bit vectors; a single error produces the corresponding column as its syndrome.
consequence: They are the simplest nontrivial family of perfect error-correcting codes.

title: Perfectness of Binary Hamming Codes
subject: Information Theory
statement: Binary Hamming codes are perfect: the radius-one Hamming balls around codewords partition the entire ambient space.
short: Every possible received word is within one bit of exactly one codeword.
detail: Perfect codes are rare; besides Hamming codes and a few Golay codes, no nontrivial perfect codes exist over finite fields.
proof: The code has 2 to the n minus m codewords, each ball has n plus one elements, and the product equals 2 to the n, so disjoint balls cover everything.
consequence: Single-error correction is optimal in the sense of the Hamming bound.

title: Reed–Solomon Codes
subject: Information Theory
statement: Reed–Solomon codes evaluate polynomials of degree less than k at n distinct field elements, yielding linear codes with minimum distance n minus k plus one.
short: Polynomial evaluation turns message coefficients into highly redundant codewords.
detail: They are maximum distance separable and are used in storage, QR codes, and deep-space communication.
proof: Two distinct polynomials of degree below k agree at fewer than k points, so their evaluations differ in at least n minus k plus one positions.
consequence: They attain the Singleton bound and support erasure correction via interpolation.

title: BCH Codes
subject: Information Theory
statement: BCH codes are cyclic codes whose generator polynomial is chosen to have prescribed consecutive powers of a primitive element as roots, guaranteeing a designed minimum distance.
short: Choosing roots of the generator polynomial forces a guaranteed distance.
detail: Binary BCH codes generalise Hamming codes and admit efficient algebraic decoding via the Berlekamp–Massey algorithm.
proof: If the generator vanishes at delta minus one consecutive powers, any codeword polynomial has those roots, and the BCH bound shows its weight is at least delta.
consequence: They provide adjustable error-correction capability with practical decoding.

title: Cyclic Codes as Polynomial Ideals
subject: Information Theory
statement: A cyclic code of length n over a finite field corresponds to an ideal in the quotient ring of polynomials modulo x to the n minus one, generated by a divisor of x to the n minus one.
short: Cyclic shifts correspond to multiplying by x modulo x to the n minus one.
detail: This algebraic view makes encoding and decoder design reduce to polynomial arithmetic.
proof: The ring is principal because it is a quotient of a polynomial ring over a field; cyclic shift invariance is multiplication by x.
consequence: It unifies the treatment of Hamming, BCH, and Reed–Solomon codes.

title: LDPC Codes and Iterative Decoding
subject: Information Theory
statement: Low-density parity-check codes have sparse parity-check matrices and are decoded by iterative message-passing algorithms that approach channel capacity in practice.
short: A sparse web of parity checks allows fast approximate inference.
detail: Gallager introduced them in the 1960s; modern irregular constructions approach the Shannon limit closely.
proof: The sparse factor graph permits local belief-propagation updates whose fixed points approximate the maximum-likelihood decoding decision.
consequence: They are used in modern communication and storage standards.

title: Turbo Codes
subject: Information Theory
statement: Turbo codes combine two or more convolutional codes with an interleaver and decode them iteratively by exchanging soft information between component decoders.
short: Two simple codes plus iteration yield near-capacity performance.
detail: They were a breakthrough in coding theory because their performance is close to the Shannon limit with manageable complexity.
proof: The interleaver spreads bursts of errors, and the exchange of posterior information between decoders improves estimates on each iteration.
consequence: They shaped practical deep-space and mobile communication systems.

title: Minimum Distance Determines Error Capability
subject: Information Theory
statement: A code with minimum Hamming distance d can detect up to d minus one errors and correct up to floor of (d minus one) over two errors.
short: Distance is the resource that error correction spends.
detail: The same bound applies to erasures with a different threshold: d minus one erasures can always be recovered.
proof: If two codewords were within 2t or fewer positions, an error pattern could transform one into the other; the packing of radius-t balls ensures unique nearest codeword.
consequence: It connects code design directly to error performance.

title: Shannon Entropy
subject: Information Theory
statement: The entropy of a discrete random variable is the expected negative logarithm of its probability, measured in bits when the logarithm base is two.
short: Entropy measures average surprise or uncertainty.
detail: A deterministic variable has entropy zero and a uniform variable over n outcomes has entropy log two of n.
proof: Definition; Jensen's inequality gives the upper bound attained exactly at the uniform distribution.
consequence: It is the basic currency of information theory.

title: Joint and Conditional Entropy
subject: Information Theory
statement: The joint entropy of two variables is the entropy of their pair, and the conditional entropy of X given Y is the expected entropy of X given each value of Y.
short: Uncertainty in two variables splits into one plus the remaining uncertainty.
detail: Conditioning can only reduce expected entropy, though knowing a particular outcome can increase it.
proof: Expand the definition of joint entropy and regroup terms using conditional probabilities.
consequence: These quantities underpin the chain rule and mutual information.

title: The Chain Rule for Entropy
subject: Information Theory
statement: The entropy of a collection of random variables equals the sum of conditional entropies of each variable given all preceding ones.
short: Total uncertainty accumulates one variable at a time.
detail: For independent variables the chain rule reduces to the sum of individual entropies.
proof: Repeatedly apply the two-variable identity H(X,Y) = H(X) + H(Y|X).
consequence: It is used throughout proofs about source coding and Markov chains.

title: Mutual Information in Information Theory
subject: Information Theory
statement: The mutual information between X and Y is the reduction in entropy of X after observing Y, equal to the Kullback–Leibler divergence between the joint distribution and the product of marginals.
short: How much one variable tells you about another.
detail: It is symmetric and nonnegative, and equals zero exactly for independent variables.
proof: Expand the definitions and compare the two expressions term by term.
consequence: It quantifies information flow in channels and learning problems.

title: Kullback–Leibler Divergence
subject: Information Theory
statement: The Kullback–Leibler divergence between probability distributions p and q is the expected log-ratio of p to q under p.
short: A measure of how far one distribution is from another.
detail: It is not symmetric and does not satisfy the triangle inequality, so it is a divergence rather than a metric.
proof: Definition; Gibbs' inequality shows it is nonnegative, with equality exactly when p and q coincide.
consequence: It appears in hypothesis testing, variational inference, and information bounds.

title: Gibbs' Inequality
subject: Information Theory
statement: For any two probability distributions p and q with p absolutely continuous with respect to q, the divergence D of p from q is nonnegative, with equality only when p equals q.
short: A distribution cannot be closer to another than to itself.
detail: The continuous analogue is proved identically using Jensen's inequality on the logarithm.
proof: Apply Jensen's inequality to the convex function negative logarithm: minus the expectation of log(q/p) is at least minus the log of the expectation of q/p, which is zero.
consequence: It justifies divergences as measures of discrepancy.

title: The Data Processing Inequality
subject: Information Theory
statement: For a Markov chain X to Y to Z, the mutual information between X and Z is at most the mutual information between X and Y.
short: Post-processing cannot create information about the original variable.
detail: Equality can hold when Z is a sufficient statistic of Y for X.
proof: Expand the chain rule in two ways and use the conditional independence of X and Z given Y to show the difference is I(Y;Z|X) or I(X;Y|Z) as appropriate, which is nonnegative.
consequence: It is a fundamental limitation in statistics, privacy, and communication.

title: Differential Entropy
subject: Information Theory
statement: Differential entropy generalizes Shannon entropy to continuous densities as the integral of minus f times the logarithm of f.
short: Continuous uncertainty has a differential analogue, but it can be negative.
detail: Unlike discrete entropy it is not invariant under arbitrary nonlinear changes of coordinates and can exceed the entropy of a discrete approximation.
proof: Definition; scaling a variable by a factor a shifts h by log of the absolute value of a.
consequence: It appears in continuous channel capacity and Gaussian rate-distortion.

title: Uniformity Maximizes Entropy
subject: Information Theory
statement: Among all distributions on a finite set of size n, the uniform distribution has the largest Shannon entropy, equal to log base two of n.
short: Uncertainty is greatest when every outcome is equally likely.
detail: More generally, fixing the support size gives the uniform maximum; with constraints such as a fixed mean, other maximum-entropy distributions arise.
proof: By Gibbs' inequality, the divergence from p to the uniform distribution is log n minus H(p), which is nonnegative.
consequence: It underlies maximum-entropy methods and the design of random sources.

title: Rate–Distortion Theory
subject: Information Theory
statement: The rate-distortion function R of D is the smallest mutual information needed between a source and its reproduction so that the expected distortion is at most D.
latex: R(D) = min_{p(x̂|x): E d ≤ D} I(X;X̂)
short: It quantifies the minimum bits needed for a given reconstruction quality.
detail: For a Gaussian source under squared-error distortion, the function has a closed form that decreases logarithmically with allowed distortion.
proof: Minimise mutual information over conditionally independent test channels satisfying the distortion constraint; the Blahut–Arimoto algorithm computes it numerically.
consequence: It sets the theoretical limit of lossy compression.

title: Huffman Coding
subject: Information Theory
statement: Huffman coding constructs an optimal prefix code by repeatedly merging the two least probable symbols or subtrees into a new node.
latex: expected length L satisfies H(X) ≤ L < H(X) + 1
short: Give short codewords to likely symbols and build the tree bottom-up.
detail: The algorithm runs in time n log n with a priority queue and can be generalized to D-ary alphabets.
proof: An optimal prefix tree has the two least likely symbols as sibling leaves at maximum depth; merging them reduces to a smaller optimal-code problem.
consequence: It achieves entropy to within one bit per symbol and is widely used in compression.

title: Arithmetic Coding
subject: Information Theory
statement: Arithmetic coding represents an entire message as a subinterval of the unit interval whose length corresponds to the probability of the message.
short: Encode a whole sequence as one fractional number rather than one codeword per symbol.
detail: It often beats Huffman coding on small alphabets and skewed distributions because it need not assign an integer number of bits per symbol.
proof: Partition the current interval into subintervals proportional to symbol probabilities and recursively narrow it; the final interval identifies the message.
consequence: It is a core technique in modern image and video compression.

title: The Kraft–McMillan Inequality
subject: Information Theory
statement: For any binary prefix code with codeword lengths lᵢ, the sum of two to the minus lᵢ is at most one; conversely any sequence of lengths satisfying this bound can be realized by a prefix code.
short: Codeword lengths must fit inside the unit interval of binary strings.
detail: The inequality is a key tool in proving optimality properties of Huffman coding.
proof: Each codeword of length l corresponds to a cylinder set of measure two to the minus l; prefix-free sets have disjoint cylinders inside a space of measure one.
consequence: It characterizes feasible code lengths for instantaneous codes.

title: Kolmogorov Complexity and Incompressibility
subject: Information Theory
statement: The Kolmogorov complexity of a string is the length of the shortest program that outputs it, and most strings of length n have complexity close to n.
short: Most strings cannot be shortened because there are too few short programs.
detail: Kolmogorov complexity is uncomputable, and its incomputability mirrors the halting problem.
proof: There are fewer than 2 to the n programs of length below n minus c, so at most a fraction two to the minus c of strings are compressible by c bits.
consequence: It gives an individual, nonprobabilistic notion of randomness and information.

title: The TCP/IP Reference Model
subject: Computer Networks
statement: The TCP/IP model organizes networking into application, transport, internet, and link layers, with each layer providing services to the one above it.
short: Four layers from user data down to physical signalling.
detail: The model is defined by its protocols rather than a strict specification; the Internet Protocol and Transmission Control Protocol are its core.
proof: Describe encapsulation: each layer adds a header and passes the result downward, and decapsulation reverses the process at the receiver.
consequence: It is the architecture underlying the practical Internet.

title: The OSI Seven-Layer Model
subject: Computer Networks
statement: The OSI model divides networking into physical, data link, network, transport, session, presentation, and application layers.
latex: physical, link, network, transport, session, presentation, application
short: A conceptual seven-layer reference for describing network functions.
detail: It is primarily a teaching and standards-reference model; real stacks such as TCP/IP do not map onto it exactly.
proof: List the layers and the service each provides, noting encapsulation between adjacent layers.
consequence: It provides common vocabulary for discussing protocols and interfaces.

title: The TCP Three-Way Handshake
subject: Computer Networks
statement: TCP establishes a connection by exchanging a SYN, a SYN-ACK, and an ACK, which synchronises initial sequence numbers on both sides.
short: Three messages let both sides agree to start a reliable connection.
detail: Because old duplicate packets may linger, both endpoints need a fresh starting sequence number verified by the handshake.
proof: Each side sends its initial sequence number and acknowledges the other's, so after three messages both know the connection is live and synchronised.
consequence: It prevents stale connections from being accepted and initializes reliable delivery.

title: TCP Congestion Control
subject: Computer Networks
statement: TCP congestion control adjusts a congestion window using acknowledgements and loss signals to probe available bandwidth without overwhelming the network.
latex: cwnd grows on ACKs, shrinks on loss
short: Send faster until loss, then back off and probe again.
detail: Classic variants include Tahoe, Reno, and NewReno; modern variants such as BBR use delay and bandwidth estimates.
proof: AIMD dynamics give convergence to a fair share of bottleneck capacity; loss is treated as a signal of queue overflow.
consequence: It is the main mechanism keeping the Internet stable under load.

title: Additive Increase Multiplicative Decrease
subject: Computer Networks
statement: AIMD increases the sending rate linearly on success and halves it on congestion, which converges to a fair and efficient allocation among competing flows.
latex: w ← w + 1 per RTT; w ← w/2 on loss
short: Probe gently, retreat sharply.
detail: The sawtooth behaviour of AIMD is the classic TCP congestion-control signature.
proof: The additive increase and multiplicative decrease rule satisfies the conditions for convergence to max-min fairness in a single bottleneck.
consequence: It explains why TCP flows tend to share bandwidth fairly.

title: Slow Start and Congestion Avoidance
subject: Computer Networks
statement: TCP slow start doubles the congestion window each round-trip time until a threshold, after which congestion avoidance increases it by one segment per round-trip time.
latex: cwnd doubles before ssthresh, then grows linearly
short: Exponential probing first, then careful linear growth.
detail: A retransmission timeout resets the window to one segment and sets the threshold to half the previous window.
proof: On each acknowledgement the window grows by one maximum segment size; during slow start each segment generates an acknowledgement, giving exponential growth.
consequence: It allows rapid startup while limiting the risk of congestion collapse.

title: Fast Retransmit and Fast Recovery
subject: Computer Networks
statement: Three duplicate acknowledgements trigger TCP fast retransmission of the missing segment without waiting for a timeout, followed by fast recovery instead of a full slow start.
short: Duplicate ACKs are a strong hint that one segment was lost.
detail: Reno's fast recovery inflates the window with each additional duplicate ACK so the pipe stays full while recovering.
proof: A duplicate ACK implies a later segment arrived out of order, so the missing segment can be retransmitted immediately.
consequence: It greatly improves throughput under isolated packet losses.

title: Sliding Window Flow Control
subject: Computer Networks
statement: Sliding-window protocols let a sender transmit up to a window of unacknowledged data, advancing the window as acknowledgements arrive.
short: Keep several packets in flight instead of waiting for each one.
detail: TCP combines the receiver's flow-control window with the sender's congestion window, using the smaller of the two.
proof: The receiver advertises free buffer space; the sender never has more than that many unacknowledged bytes outstanding.
consequence: It improves throughput while preventing a fast sender from overwhelming a slow receiver.

title: Go-Back-N and Selective Repeat
subject: Computer Networks
statement: Go-Back-N retransmits the lost packet and all subsequent packets, while selective repeat retransmits only the packets that were not acknowledged.
latex: GBN: retransmit from lost packet; SR: retransmit missing packets
short: Simple retransmission versus efficient but more complex retransmission.
detail: Selective repeat requires out-of-order buffering at the receiver and larger sequence-number space.
proof: In Go-Back-N the receiver accepts only the next expected packet and discards later ones; selective repeat buffers later packets and requests only gaps.
consequence: They illustrate the tradeoff between implementation simplicity and bandwidth efficiency.

title: IP and Best-Effort Delivery
subject: Computer Networks
statement: The Internet Protocol provides connectionless, best-effort delivery of datagrams, with no guarantees of delivery, order, or duplicate suppression.
short: Packets may be lost, reordered, or duplicated.
detail: Reliability, ordering, and flow control are provided by higher-layer protocols such as TCP.
proof: Routers forward each datagram independently using a time-to-live field to prevent infinite loops, without maintaining per-flow state.
consequence: The simple service model allows a wide variety of transport protocols.

title: IPv4 and IPv6 Address Spaces
subject: Computer Networks
statement: IPv4 uses 32-bit addresses while IPv6 uses 128-bit addresses, vastly expanding the number of available identifiers.
short: IPv6 solves address exhaustion with a much larger space.
detail: IPv6 also simplifies header processing and removes the checksum, but is not backwards compatible with IPv4.
proof: Compare the address field lengths of the two header formats.
consequence: IPv6 deployment is driven mainly by address exhaustion.

title: Network Address Translation
subject: Computer Networks
statement: NAT maps private IP addresses inside a local network to a smaller number of public addresses by rewriting packet headers and tracking active connections.
short: Many internal hosts share one public address.
detail: Port-aware NAT lets multiple hosts share a single address but complicates inbound connections and peer-to-peer protocols.
proof: Maintain a translation table keyed by internal address and port, and rewrite source fields on outbound packets and destination fields on inbound ones.
consequence: It delayed IPv4 exhaustion and is ubiquitous in home and enterprise routers.

title: CIDR and Subnetting
subject: Computer Networks
statement: Classless Inter-Domain Routing represents an address block by a prefix and length, allowing flexible aggregation of routes and subdivision of address spaces.
short: A prefix length replaces rigid address classes.
detail: CIDR enables route aggregation, which keeps routing tables manageable.
proof: Interpret the address as a bit string and use the prefix length as the number of significant bits in a longest-prefix match.
consequence: It is essential to scalable routing and efficient address allocation.

title: DNS Hierarchical Name Resolution
subject: Computer Networks
statement: The Domain Name System maps human-readable hostnames to IP addresses using a distributed hierarchy of root, top-level, authoritative, and recursive resolvers with caching.
short: A global distributed directory translates names into addresses.
detail: Records have time-to-live values that control caching, and DNSSEC can authenticate responses.
proof: A resolver queries servers from the root down the hierarchy until an authoritative answer is found, caching intermediate results.
consequence: It is a critical piece of Internet infrastructure.

title: BGP and Path-Vector Routing
subject: Computer Networks
statement: The Border Gateway Protocol is the Internet's inter-domain routing protocol; each autonomous system advertises reachable prefixes with the path of autonomous systems it would traverse.
short: Routers choose paths based on policies and advertised AS sequences.
detail: BGP emphasises policy and scalability over shortest paths and can take time to converge after failures.
proof: Each update carries an AS path; an AS ignores routes containing itself, preventing loops, and local policies select the preferred route.
consequence: It holds the global routing system together.

title: OSPF and Link-State Routing
subject: Computer Networks
statement: OSPF is an interior link-state protocol in which routers flood information about their neighbours and compute shortest paths with Dijkstra's algorithm.
short: Every router builds a full map and computes its own routes.
detail: Areas limit the size of the link-state database; Hello packets detect neighbour failures.
proof: Flooding gives every router in an area the same graph, and Dijkstra's algorithm computes shortest paths from that router to all others.
consequence: It converges quickly and supports scalable intra-domain routing.

title: Distance-Vector Routing and Count to Infinity
subject: Computer Networks
statement: Distance-vector protocols can take many iterations to recover from a link failure, with routing metrics increasing toward infinity; split horizon and poison reverse mitigate this.
short: Neighbours can reinforce each other's stale bad news.
detail: Routing Information Protocol uses a hop-count limit of fifteen to bound the problem.
proof: After a route disappears, two routers may each believe the other has a path, incrementing the metric in turn until the maximum is reached.
consequence: It motivates the use of link-state or path-vector protocols in larger networks.

title: Ethernet and CSMA/CD
subject: Computer Networks
statement: Classic shared-medium Ethernet uses carrier sense multiple access with collision detection: a station listens before sending and detects collisions while transmitting.
short: Listen before talking, stop and retry if two talk at once.
detail: A random backoff after a collision reduces repeated collisions; switched full-duplex Ethernet no longer needs CSMA/CD.
proof: Stations sense the medium and transmit; if simultaneous transmissions corrupt a frame, all detect the collision and jam before backing off randomly.
consequence: It explains the design of early LANs and minimum frame-size requirements.
