title: The Spanning Tree Protocol
subject: Computer Networks
statement: The Spanning Tree Protocol prevents loops in bridged Ethernet networks by blocking ports so that the active topology is a tree.
short: Keep redundant links but disable some until needed.
detail: If an active link fails, the protocol unblocks a previously disabled port to restore connectivity.
proof: Switches elect a root bridge and compute shortest paths to it; ports not on those paths are blocked, eliminating cycles.
consequence: It allows physical redundancy without broadcast storms.

title: MAC Address Learning in Switches
subject: Computer Networks
statement: An Ethernet switch learns which port leads to each MAC address by inspecting source addresses of incoming frames and uses that table to forward future frames selectively.
short: Switches learn where devices live by watching their traffic.
detail: Unknown destination addresses are flooded; table entries expire after a timeout to handle moved devices.
proof: Record source address and incoming port; on forwarding, look up the destination and send only to the matching port.
consequence: It makes switched Ethernet far more efficient than shared hubs.

title: ARP and Neighbor Discovery
subject: Computer Networks
statement: The Address Resolution Protocol maps IPv4 addresses to link-layer MAC addresses on a local network; IPv6 uses Neighbor Discovery instead.
short: Find the hardware address of the next hop on this link.
detail: ARP operates by broadcasting a request and caching the reply, which makes it vulnerable to spoofing without defenses.
proof: A host broadcasts who owns a given IP address and the owner replies with its MAC address, which is then cached.
consequence: It bridges the network and link layers.

title: The End-to-End Principle
subject: Computer Networks
statement: The end-to-end principle says that application-level functions should be implemented at the communicating endpoints rather than inside the network whenever possible.
short: Keep the network simple and let hosts do the clever work.
detail: It explains why TCP ensures reliability even though the IP layer is unreliable; middleboxes such as NAT are practical exceptions.
proof: Only endpoints have complete knowledge of the application's needs, and duplicating functions inside the network cannot make them fully correct.
consequence: It has shaped Internet architecture and debates about network neutrality.

title: Hidden Node Problem and RTS/CTS
subject: Computer Networks
statement: In a wireless network two stations out of range of each other may transmit to the same access point simultaneously and collide, since neither senses the other.
latex: hidden terminals cause collisions at receiver
short: Not hearing a neighbour does not mean not interfering with it.
detail: The RTS/CTS exchange reserves the medium around the receiver and reduces collisions for large frames.
proof: Station A cannot sense B but both reach the access point; simultaneous transmissions overlap there, so a collision occurs despite clear carrier sense at each sender.
consequence: It motivated the design of wireless medium-access protocols.

title: Software-Defined Networking
subject: Computer Networks
statement: Software-defined networking separates the control plane that decides routes from the data plane that forwards packets, centralising routing decisions in a controller.
latex: control plane separated from data plane
short: One logical controller tells switches how to forward traffic.
detail: OpenFlow is a standard interface between controller and switches; benefits include programmability and easier management.
proof: Switches forward according to flow tables installed by the controller, so changing policy does not require changing each device's distributed routing algorithm.
consequence: It enables flexible, centrally managed networks.

title: The Von Neumann Architecture
subject: Computer Architecture
statement: The von Neumann architecture stores both program instructions and data in the same addressable memory, with a processor that fetches and executes instructions sequentially.
latex: CPU ↔ unified memory for code and data
short: Instructions are data, so a program can be stored and modified like any other information.
detail: This stored-program idea enables general-purpose computers but also creates the instruction-fetch bottleneck.
proof: Describe the cycle: fetch an instruction from the address in the program counter, decode it, execute it, and update the counter.
consequence: It is the blueprint of almost every general-purpose computer today.

title: The Harvard Architecture
subject: Computer Architecture
statement: The Harvard architecture keeps instruction memory and data memory physically separate, allowing simultaneous access to both.
short: Two memories mean instructions and data can be fetched in parallel.
detail: Modern processors often use a modified Harvard design: separate level-one caches but a shared main memory.
proof: Because the two memories have distinct address spaces and buses, instruction fetch and data access do not conflict.
consequence: It is common in embedded processors and digital signal processors.

title: RISC and CISC Instruction Sets
subject: Computer Architecture
statement: RISC architectures use a small set of simple instructions with load-store memory access, while CISC architectures provide richer instructions that may perform multi-step operations.
latex: RISC: simple, regular; CISC: complex, dense
short: Keep instructions simple and fast, or expressive and compact.
detail: The distinction has blurred as CISC processors translate complex instructions into internal micro-operations and RISC processors add specialised instructions.
proof: Compare instruction formats, addressing modes, and memory access rules of representative designs.
consequence: The tradeoff shapes compiler design and pipeline implementation.

title: The Fetch–Decode–Execute Cycle
subject: Computer Architecture
statement: A processor repeatedly fetches the instruction addressed by the program counter, decodes its opcode and operands, executes it, and updates the program counter.
short: The CPU's heartbeat is one instruction at a time.
detail: Pipelining overlaps these stages for different instructions, raising throughput without reducing single-instruction latency.
proof: Describe how control signals drive the datapath through each stage and how branches modify the program counter.
consequence: It is the foundation for understanding instruction-level parallelism.

title: Instruction Pipelining
subject: Computer Architecture
statement: Pipelining overlaps the execution of several instructions by dividing processing into stages, so ideally one instruction completes per cycle after the pipeline fills.
short: Like an assembly line, different instructions occupy different stages at once.
detail: Actual speedup is limited by hazards, pipeline-register overhead, and imperfect branch prediction.
proof: With k balanced stages and a steady stream of instructions, one stage completes per clock after an initial latency of k cycles.
consequence: It is the primary technique for increasing processor throughput.

title: Pipeline Hazards
subject: Computer Architecture
statement: Pipeline hazards are situations preventing the next instruction from executing in its designated cycle: structural resource conflicts, data dependencies, and control dependencies from branches.
short: An assembly line stalls when the next task needs an unavailable result or a different route.
detail: Data hazards are mitigated by forwarding and scheduling; control hazards by prediction; structural hazards by duplicating resources.
proof: Classify dependencies between instructions and show that without intervention the required value or resource is not ready at the needed stage.
consequence: Hazards determine the real speedup of a pipeline.

title: Branch Prediction
subject: Computer Architecture
statement: Branch prediction guesses the outcome of a conditional branch so the pipeline can keep fetching without waiting for the branch to resolve.
short: Guess where the program will go and recover if wrong.
detail: Dynamic predictors use branch-history tables and two-bit saturating counters; a wrong guess flushes wrongly fetched instructions.
proof: Maintain history indexed by branch address and update it with actual outcomes; accuracy above the misprediction threshold yields a speedup.
consequence: Accurate prediction is essential for deep pipelines.

title: Superscalar Execution
subject: Computer Architecture
statement: A superscalar processor issues multiple independent instructions per clock cycle to duplicated functional units.
short: More than one instruction can start on every tick.
detail: Finding enough independent instructions requires wide issue logic, register renaming, and aggressive prediction.
proof: Provide multiple execution units and issue logic that checks dependencies before issuing instructions in the same cycle.
consequence: It raises throughput beyond what a single pipeline can deliver.

title: Out-of-Order Execution and Tomasulo's Algorithm
subject: Computer Architecture
statement: Tomasulo's algorithm allows instructions to execute as soon as their operands are ready, using reservation stations and register renaming to avoid false dependencies.
short: Execute ready instructions first and rename registers to remove spurious waits.
detail: Results are broadcast on a common data bus to all waiting reservation stations, and retirement logic preserves precise exceptions.
proof: Rename destination registers to tags, issue instructions to reservation stations, and broadcast results so dependent instructions wake up.
consequence: It is a foundational technique for exploiting instruction-level parallelism.

title: The Memory Hierarchy
subject: Computer Architecture
statement: The memory hierarchy arranges storage from fast small registers and caches through main memory to slow large secondary storage, exploiting locality to close the speed gap.
short: Keep frequently used data close to the processor.
detail: Each level trades capacity and cost for latency; effective performance depends on hit rates at each level.
proof: Locality implies that recent or nearby data is likely to be reused, so keeping a small fast copy gives most of the benefit of a large slow store.
consequence: It is central to computer performance.

title: Locality of Reference
subject: Computer Architecture
statement: Programs tend to access the same locations repeatedly (temporal locality) and nearby locations soon after (spatial locality).
short: Recent and neighbouring data are likely to be needed again.
detail: Caches, virtual memory, and prefetching all rely on this empirical property.
proof: Observed program behaviour shows loops and sequential traversal; these yield repeated and clustered access patterns.
consequence: It justifies caches and many performance optimizations.

title: Cache Lines and Spatial Locality
subject: Computer Architecture
statement: Caches transfer data in blocks called cache lines, so fetching one word also brings in neighbouring words that may be used soon.
short: Fetch a block, not a single word.
detail: Larger lines exploit spatial locality but increase miss penalties and can cause false sharing between cores.
proof: Memory is addressed by line; a miss loads the whole line containing the requested word.
consequence: Line size is a key cache design parameter.

title: Direct-Mapped and Set-Associative Caches
subject: Computer Architecture
statement: A direct-mapped cache places each memory block in exactly one cache line, while a k-way set-associative cache allows a block in any of k lines within one set.
short: Simplicity versus fewer conflict misses.
detail: Fully associative caches allow any block anywhere but require more comparison hardware.
proof: Partition the address into tag, set index, and offset; direct mapping uses one line per set, associativity uses k.
consequence: Associativity trades hardware cost against hit rate.

title: The Three Cs of Cache Misses
subject: Computer Architecture
statement: Cache misses are classified as compulsory misses on first access, capacity misses because the cache is too small, and conflict misses because of mapping collisions.
short: Three distinct reasons a lookup can fail.
detail: The classification guides optimizations such as prefetching, larger caches, and higher associativity.
proof: Partition misses by whether the block was everaccessed, whether it was evicted because of total size, or because of set contention.
consequence: It provides a vocabulary for cache-performance analysis.

title: Cache Coherence and the MESI Protocol
subject: Computer Architecture
statement: MESI is a cache-coherence protocol giving each cached line one of four states: modified, exclusive, shared, or invalid, so multiple cores see a consistent view of memory.
short: Track who owns and may modify each cached line.
detail: Write-invalidate protocols broadcast invalidations on writes; directory-based schemes scale this to many cores.
proof: Transitions on reads, writes, and snoops ensure at most one modified copy and that any shared copies agree with memory.
consequence: It underpins correct shared-memory multiprocessing.

title: Write-Back versus Write-Through Caches
subject: Computer Architecture
statement: Write-through caches update main memory on every write, while write-back caches mark a line dirty and write it to memory only on eviction.
short: Update memory immediately or postpone until eviction.
detail: Write-back reduces memory traffic but requires dirty bits and more complex coherence handling.
proof: With write-back, the cache line holds the only valid copy of modified data until it is written back, so a dirty bit records the need.
consequence: The choice affects bandwidth, latency, and coherence complexity.

title: Virtual Memory and Paging
subject: Computer Architecture
statement: Virtual memory gives each process a large private address space divided into fixed-size pages, which are mapped to physical frames by a page table and loaded on demand.
short: Programs see a big private memory; the OS maps it to real pages.
detail: A page fault occurs when a referenced page is not resident, causing the operating system to fetch it from disk.
proof: The memory management unit translates virtual addresses via the page table; demand paging loads pages only when first accessed.
consequence: It enables isolation, memory overcommitment, and simpler programming.

title: Translation Lookaside Buffers
subject: Computer Architecture
statement: A translation lookaside buffer is a small cache of recent virtual-to-physical address translations that avoids walking the page table on every memory access.
short: Cache address translations just as caches data.
detail: A TLB miss requires a page-table walk, which is costly; large pages reduce TLB pressure.
proof: Check the TLB first; on a hit, combine the cached frame number with the page offset to form the physical address.
consequence: TLB performance can dominate memory-access time.

title: Amdahl's Law
subject: Computer Architecture
statement: The maximum speedup from parallelizing a fraction p of a computation by a factor s is one divided by the sum of the unparallelized fraction and p over s.
short: The serial part of a program limits the gains from parallelism.
detail: As s grows the speedup approaches 1/(1−p), so even a small serial fraction caps performance.
proof: Let total work be one unit; after acceleration the time is (1−p) plus p/s, and speedup is the reciprocal.
consequence: It explains why adding processors has diminishing returns.

title: Gustafson's Law
subject: Computer Architecture
statement: Gustafson's law argues that with a fixed time budget, scaling the problem size with the number of processors gives speedup of the form (1−p) plus p times the number of processors.
short: Bigger machines can tackle bigger problems in the same time.
detail: It offers a more optimistic view than Amdahl's law by allowing the parallel portion to grow with available hardware.
proof: Normalize the serial fraction in the scaled workload and observe that the parallel part grows linearly with the number of processors.
consequence: It motivates weak scaling in parallel performance evaluation.

title: Flynn's Taxonomy
subject: Computer Architecture
statement: Flynn's taxonomy classifies architectures by the number of instruction and data streams: SISD, SIMD, MISD, and MIMD.
short: Count instruction streams and data streams.
detail: Most modern systems are MIMD, often with SIMD units inside each core.
proof: Define the four combinations of single or multiple instruction and data streams.
consequence: It provides a simple vocabulary for parallel machines.

title: SIMD and Vector Processing
subject: Computer Architecture
statement: SIMD execution applies one instruction to many data elements in parallel using wide vector registers or lanes.
latex: one operation on a vector of elements
short: Do the same thing to many pieces of data at once.
detail: It is highly effective for multimedia, scientific kernels, and machine learning, but requires regular data parallelism.
proof: Broadcast a single instruction to multiple functional lanes operating on different register elements.
consequence: It delivers energy-efficient throughput for data-parallel code.

title: The PRAM Parallel Model
subject: Computer Architecture
statement: The parallel random-access machine model consists of many processors sharing a global memory, distinguished by whether concurrent reads and writes are allowed.
short: An idealized shared-memory parallel computer.
detail: Algorithms are analysed by parallel time and processor count, with work as their product.
proof: Define processors with local registers and shared memory, and specify conflict rules for concurrent accesses.
consequence: It is a standard theoretical model for parallel algorithms.

title: The Bulk Synchronous Parallel Model
subject: Computer Architecture
statement: The bulk synchronous parallel model organizes computation into supersteps in which processors perform local work, communicate, and then synchronise at a barrier.
short: Compute locally, exchange messages, then meet at a barrier.
detail: Its cost model accounts for computation time, communication volume, and synchronisation overhead, making it more realistic than PRAM.
proof: Analyse each superstep as a sequence of local computation, routing of messages, and a global barrier before the next step.
consequence: It underpins practical parallel frameworks such as Pregel.

title: The Von Neumann Bottleneck
subject: Computer Architecture
statement: The von Neumann bottleneck is the limited rate at which data can be transferred between processor and memory, which can leave fast processors idle waiting for instructions or operands.
short: Compute is fast but feeding it is slow.
detail: Caches, prefetching, and wider buses mitigate but do not remove the limitation.
proof: Compare processor cycle time with memory latency and bandwidth; when memory cannot keep up, the pipeline stalls.
consequence: It motivates most of modern memory-hierarchy design.

title: The Roofline Model
subject: Computer Architecture
statement: The roofline model bounds achievable performance by the smaller of peak arithmetic throughput and memory bandwidth multiplied by arithmetic intensity.
short: A kernel is compute-bound or memory-bound depending on its arithmetic intensity.
detail: Arithmetic intensity is operations per byte of memory traffic; the model gives a visual ceiling for optimizing kernels.
proof: A kernel needing I operations per byte cannot exceed bandwidth times I, and cannot exceed the processor's peak operation rate.
consequence: It guides performance tuning on modern processors and accelerators.
